readerTitle: Does a packed restaurant have network effects?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당, 부품 제조업체, 매장 근무 앱) · 유닛 개념 적용 레슨
insight: 인기가 인기를 부르는 것처럼 보여도, 손님 한 명이 늘 때 다른 손님이 얻는 가치가 커지지 않으면 네트워크 효과가 아니다.
misconception: 줄 서는 식당이나 고객이 많을수록 원가가 내려가는 회사는 네트워크 효과를 가진 것이다.

sources.text: PIXO BMO-04-01 Direct network effects, BMO-04-05 When networks get worse (유닛 개념 레슨)

factChecks.note: 실제 통계나 기업 사실은 쓰지 않았습니다. 모든 장면은 가상 사례입니다.
'네트워크 효과 = 사용자가 늘수록 기존 사용자에게 가치가 커지는 것', '규모의 경제(원가 하락)·사회적 증거(줄이 신호)는 네트워크 효과가 아니다'라는 구분이 BMO-04-01, BMO-04-05의 정의·용어와 일치하는지 확인하세요.
6번 카드의 바·클럽 예시(손님 자체가 경험의 일부)는 일반적 설명으로만 썼습니다. 특정 연구나 수치를 덧붙이지 마세요.

cards.title: Does a packed restaurant have network effects?
body: Two noodle shops sit side by side. One has a line out the door. The other has empty tables.
Most people join the line. So more customers bring even more customers. That sounds like a network effect. Today you'll test whether it really is one.

image.label: Two noodle shops, one with a long line, one empty
image.brief: 나란히 붙은 국숫집 두 곳. 왼쪽 가게 앞에는 긴 줄, 오른쪽 가게는 빈 테이블과 심심한 직원. 따뜻한 저녁 조명, 일러스트 스타일. 실제 상호나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Is the line a network effect?
body: You own the busy noodle shop. A friend says, "You've got network effects. The more people eat here, the more people want to."

options.text: Yes. Crowds attract crowds, so value grows with every customer
options.feedback: Crowds attract attention, but that's not the test. In a **direct network effect**, each new user makes the product better for existing users. An extra diner doesn't make your noodles better for anyone.

options.text: No. The line tells people the food is good, but extra diners make each meal a little worse
options.feedback: Right. The line is a signal, not a network. And with fixed seats and one kitchen, more diners mean longer waits. That's the crowding from **when networks get worse**, without any network benefit first.

options.text: Partly. It's a network effect until the shop is full
options.feedback: Good instinct that capacity matters. But even when half empty, a new diner doesn't improve your meal. The draw is information about quality, not added value from other users.

cards.title: Ask one question about the next customer.
body: A **direct network effect** means each new user makes the product more valuable to the users already there. A phone is the classic case: every new owner is someone else you can call.
So ask: *if one more person joins, do I get something I didn't have before?* At the noodle shop, you don't. Your bowl tastes the same. Your seat is no better.
What the line gives you is information. Other people's choices hint that the food is good. That's useful, but it's not a network.

image.label: Phone network grows links; restaurant just gets busier
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽: 전화기 사람 아이콘이 늘수록 서로 잇는 선이 많아짐("More links"). 오른쪽: 식당 테이블에 사람이 늘수록 시계 아이콘의 대기 시간만 길어짐("Longer wait"). 단순한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: More diners can only make it worse.
body: In real networks, growth helps users at first. Later, crowding can cut into that value. That's the idea in **when networks get worse**.
A restaurant skips the first part and goes straight to the second. Each extra diner adds to the wait, the noise and the kitchen's workload. Past a point, regulars start going elsewhere.
That's why a busy restaurant has to keep earning its line with food and service. The crowd doesn't lock anyone in.

cards.title: An investor calls it a network effect.
body: You run a machine-parts factory with 40 business clients. As you've grown, steel suppliers give you better prices, so your costs per part keep falling.
An investor says, "More clients, lower costs. That's a network effect." How do you answer?

options.text: Agree. Growth makes the whole business stronger
options.feedback: It does make you stronger, but calling it a network effect sets the wrong expectations. Rivals can match lower costs by growing too.

options.text: Call it cost savings from size, not a network effect
options.feedback: Right. Client 41 doesn't make your parts more useful to client 1. That fails the **direct network effect** test. Bigger buyers can win the same discount.

options.text: Say it's a network effect only if you pass the savings on to clients
options.feedback: Lower prices help clients, but the value still comes from your costs, not from other clients joining. The label stays wrong.

cards.title: Some venues come close, but they hit a ceiling fast.
body: In a bar or a dance club, other guests are part of what you came for. An empty room feels dead, so a few more people do make the night better.
But the room has a fixed size. Soon crowding takes over, and **when networks get worse** kicks in quickly. That small, capped effect is nothing like a network that grows across a city or a country.
So be careful with the label. Calling popularity or scale a network effect can make a business look safer than it is.

image.label: Bar that gets better, then too crowded
image.brief: 바 내부 3컷: 거의 빈 바(지루함), 적당히 붐비는 바(웃는 손님들), 꽉 찬 바(밀치는 손님, 주문 못 하는 사람). 아래에 올라갔다 금방 꺾이는 곡선. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Which feature creates a real network effect?
body: You build a scheduling app for restaurant chains. Today each manager uses it alone to plan shifts.
You can build one feature next. Which one would give the app a real network effect?

options.text: Workers can swap shifts with staff at any branch in their chain
options.feedback: Each worker who joins is one more person you can swap with. That passes the **direct network effect** test. Watch for too many swap requests later, the crowding from **when networks get worse**.

options.text: Better staffing forecasts as more restaurants share data
options.feedback: This can improve the product as it grows, but the gain often levels off. It's weaker and slower than users directly helping each other.

options.text: Volume discounts for chains with more locations
options.feedback: Good pricing, but it's a discount, not a network. One chain joining doesn't make the app more useful to another.

cards.title: A line is not a network.
body: Today you used two ideas. **Direct network effects:** does the next customer add value for the others? **When networks get worse:** does growth bring crowding? A restaurant fails the first test and meets the second right away.
**Try it today:** pick one thing that grows with your customer count. Ask whether the next customer adds value for the others, or only for you.
